Growth trajectories in Amblyopsis spelaea have been characterized through mark-recapture studies and laboratory rearing. The maximum standard length recorded for adults in the Mammoth Cave system reaches 8.8 centimeters [Li = 8.8 centimeters], a value derived from a total length of approximately 11 cm using the established relationship where standard length equals 0.8 times total length. Sexual maturity is attained when individuals reach a standard length of 5 cm [Lp = 5 cm], a threshold that corresponds to the size range of 45 to 56 mm reported in specimen-based analyses. At this developmental milestone, the average wet weight at puberty is 1.7 grams [Wwp = 1.7 grams], a body mass that is reached through an allometric scaling relationship with the ultimate length, marking a key transition in the slow life history of this cave-dwelling species. Field surveys indicate that the species maintains extremely low metabolic rates, an adaptation to the oligotrophic cave environment where food resources are scarce and temperatures remain stable.

Reproductive output in the Northern cavefish has been documented from captive populations maintained under controlled thermal regimes. At a constant ambient temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the maximum reproductive output is partitioned into distinct components: gravid females typically produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with each clutch containing around 70 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing around 70 eggs], a combination that results in a relatively low annual reproductive output compared to epigean cypriniforms. This modest fecundity reflects the energetic constraints imposed by the resource-poor subterranean habitat. The demersal eggs are large and yolk-rich, an investment that enhances the survival prospects of the yolk-sac larvae upon emergence from the chorionated embryos.

The developmental timeline from fertilisation to hatching has been studied in detail under laboratory conditions. At the stable temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], which reflects the natural thermal conditions of their groundwater habitat, the incubation period extends to approximately 168 days [ab = approximately 168 days], representing about 5.5 months of embryonic development. This prolonged period of yolk-dependence within the egg is among the longest documented for any troglobitic fish species. The wet weight at birth is exceedingly small, with newly emerged yolk-sac larvae weighing only 0.0052 grams [Wwb = 0.0052 grams], a minute mass derived from the spherical egg diameter of 2.15 mm. After chorion rupture, the prolarvae remain in an endotrophic phase, absorbing their substantial yolk reserves before the onset of first exogenous feeding at around five to six months post-hatching.

Longevity in this obligate cave-dweller is exceptional for a fish of its size. At the ambient temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded in natural populations is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years], a duration that far exceeds predictions based on body size alone among related amblyopsid species. The ultimate body mass of fully grown adults reaches 6.9 grams [Wwi = 6.9 grams], a value calculated from the length-mass allometry equation specific to this species. This combination of extreme longevity and modest adult size suggests a life history strategy heavily skewed toward somatic persistence at the expense of rapid reproduction, a classic syndrome observed in resource-limited cave environments where senescence is delayed and mortality rates are low.

The onset of reproduction occurs late relative to the species life span, reflecting a slow maturation schedule typical of extreme troglobionts. At the stable thermal regime of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the time since birth at puberty is estimated at 1281 days [tp = 1281 days], equivalent to roughly 42 months of post-hatching development before gravid females are observed spawning. This prolonged prereproductive period allows individuals to accumulate sufficient body reserves to produce the large, nutrient-rich eggs described earlier. Comparisons with other members of the family Amblyopsidae indicate that this late maturation and reduced fecundity are characteristic of a life history finely tuned to the stable but energetically restrictive conditions of the subterranean aquatic environment.
